parts.note: the theatre call summoning actors who open a play, reread as a description of young women making their first entrance into society

explanation.surface: A stage manager calls the opening cast to the wings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beginners, please!' is the backstage call before curtain-up; here the beginners are girls coming out into society for the first time.
explanation.definitionFit: Young women making their formal entry into fashionable society are newcomers, beginners in that world.

parts.note: the knight is Lancelot of the Lake, in French '...', and a French-born illustrator, Edmund, had that surname

explanation.surface: Imagining the Arthurian knight taking up a paintbrush.
explanation.walkthrough: Lancelot du Lac is the knight's French title; Edmund Dulac was a French-British book illustrator of the early 20th century.
explanation.definitionFit: The knight's French epithet 'of the Lake' is also the surname of a celebrated illustrator.

definitions.meaning: with no truce, the guns keep shelling
a bass tuba of the brass section of a band

explanation.surface: Senior officers refuse to call a ceasefire.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The brass' reads as military top brass but is the brass section; split, the instrument says 'bombard on', carry on shelling.
explanation.definitionFit: Keeping up the shelling with no truce is 'bombard on'; and a large bass tuba of military bands has that name.

clue.text: Not that the Puseyites aimed them at The Thunderer!

definitions.text: Not that the Puseyites aimed them at The Thunderer!

parts.words: Not that the Puseyites aimed them at The Thunderer!
parts.note: Pusey's Oxford Movement published pamphlets 'for the Times'; The Thunderer is the nickname of The Times, so they were for it, not aimed at it

explanation.surface: A denial that High Church Victorians attacked a newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: The Oxford Movement of Pusey and Newman published a series of pamphlets called Tracts for the Times; The Thunderer is the nickname of The Times newspaper.
explanation.definitionFit: Short religious pamphlets were the Oxford Movement's publications, issued 'for the Times'.

clue.text: Music suited to the last course

definitions.text: Music suited to the last course

parts.words: Music suited to the last course
parts.note: suited hints at Tchaikovsky's ballet suite, and the last course of dinner is dessert, when nuts are cracked

explanation.surface: Background music chosen for the end of a meal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Suited' is a pun on Tchaikovsky's ballet suite; nuts come with dessert, hence a tool for the last course.
explanation.definitionFit: Tchaikovsky's ballet suite bears the name of the tool used to open nuts at dessert.

clue.text: Hunger compelled the sale of his inheritance

definitions.text: Hunger compelled the sale of his inheritance

parts.words: Hunger compelled the sale of his inheritance
parts.note: in Genesis a famished man sold his birthright to his younger twin Jacob for a bowl of pottage

explanation.surface: Poverty forced an heir to sell off what he was left.
explanation.walkthrough: Genesis 25: the elder twin, faint with hunger, sold his birthright to Jacob for a mess of pottage.
explanation.definitionFit: Jacob's elder twin traded his birthright for food when starving, as Genesis tells.

parts.note: the instrument seems musical or scientific, but it is a toothed tool for setting hair in a neat wave

explanation.surface: A device for producing a fine ripple, perhaps at sea or in music.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wave' suggests the sea or sound; it is a hairstyle, and the tool that sets it.
explanation.definitionFit: A toothed grooming tool is what you run through hair to set a wave in it; with paper it is also a humble musical instrument.

parts.note: flighty reads as giddy, but means able to fly; a young nocturnal bird sleeps through the day

explanation.surface: A scatterbrained child lost in reverie.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flighty' and 'day-dreamer' suggest a scatterbrain; they describe a small bird that flies and sleeps by day.
explanation.definitionFit: A young owl is little, takes wing, and dreams through the daylight hours.

clue.text: Successful silk seems to be the haggling type

definitions.meaning: a silk is a King's Counsel; one doing well at the Bar gains there
one who haggles over a price

explanation.surface: A thriving barrister turns out to drive a hard bargain.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'silk' is a senior barrister (King's Counsel wear silk gowns); one who gains at the Bar is a 'bar gainer'.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who haggles over terms strikes deals; split, the word describes a lawyer winning at the Bar.

clue.text: Artist's model took a rest, or continued working

definitions.text: Artist's model took a rest, or continued working

parts.words: Artist's model took a rest, or continued working
parts.note: the word can mean rested, or, split with a hyphen after its first two letters, posed again for the painter

explanation.surface: A painter's sitter either had a break or kept going.
explanation.walkthrough: The one word covers both: rested, and 're-posed', posed once more.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means lay at rest; read with a hyphen it means sat for the artist again.

definitions.meaning: the Italian for 'my' with a feminine noun is ...
Keats's narrative poem about a serpent-woman enchantress bears this title

explanation.surface: A title like a translated poem, 'My Italian Witch', attributed to Keats.
explanation.definitionFit: Italian 'la mia' means my, run together into one word; and Keats named his poem about a serpent sorceress after her.

parts.note: Robert Louis Stevenson wrote Travels with a Donkey in the Cevennes, and Modestine was the donkey he journeyed with

explanation.surface: A literary figure in the company of his famous companion.
explanation.walkthrough: Modestine is the donkey in Stevenson's book Travels with a Donkey in the Cevennes, so Stevenson with her is a journeying man.
explanation.definitionFit: Stevenson walking the Cevennes with his donkey was a wayfarer, one making a journey.

clue.text: Is always talking of top outfitter in the Civil Service

indicators.note: the outfitter sits within the two letters for the Civil Service

parts.note: CS is the standard abbreviation for the Civil Service
a hatter supplies top hats and other headgear, outfitting the top of the body

explanation.surface: A gossip in a government office talks endlessly about a fashionable tailor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Top outfitter' reads as 'best tailor' but means one who fits out your top, a hat-maker.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who prattles on without stopping is forever gabbing, the verb in its third person form.

parts.note: in The Merchant of Venice Shylock hails the disguised lawyer as 'a Daniel come to judgment'; that lawyer was a woman, so a female Daniel

explanation.surface: A girl named Daniella on holiday in Venice.
explanation.walkthrough: Shylock calls the young 'lawyer' 'A Daniel come to judgment!'; since the lawyer is Shakespeare's heroine in disguise, she is a Daniella.
explanation.definitionFit: The heroine of The Merchant of Venice judges the case wisely, as the biblical Daniel did, and is female.

parts.note: in the pantomime the fairy godmother turns mice into the animals that pull the pumpkin carriage

explanation.surface: What happened to the mouse in the fairy tale.
explanation.walkthrough: In Cinderella the fairy godmother turns mice into the animals that draw the pumpkin carriage.
explanation.definitionFit: The mouse is magically changed into one of the animals pulling Cinderella's carriage.

clue.text: Lamb is a pet, but rebellious

definitions.meaning: a lamb reared by hand as a pet has a special dialect name
the leader of the Kentish rebellion of 1450 was named Jack ...

explanation.surface: A tame lamb that nonetheless turns unruly.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense is a name: Jack Cade led a rebellion against Henry VI in 1450.
explanation.definitionFit: A hand-reared lamb has this dialect name; and the leader of the 1450 rising against the crown bore it as his surname.

definitions.note: the clue gives an adjective; the answer is the aromatic plant it describes

indicators.note: something in a mess is jumbled up, so the letters of record in a are shuffled

explanation.surface: A gramophone disc lying in a jumble with something hot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In a mess' looks like the whole indicator, but 'in a' is part of the fodder: RECORD + IN A rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: An aromatic herb whose seeds and leaves are a spice is aptly called spicy.

parts.note: sound reads as 'healthy' or 'reliable', but it is noise that comes back reflected off a surface

explanation.surface: A sensible profit on an investment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sound return' looks like a safe investment yield; it is noise bouncing back.
explanation.definitionFit: Noise reflected back from a cliff or wall is literally a return of sound.

indicators.note: doing something unwisely means doing it carelessly, so the letters of wined are thrown about

explanation.surface: The hero of a detective story drank too much over dinner.
explanation.walkthrough: The hero of Dickens's unfinished The Mystery of Edwin Drood; 'unwisely' rearranges WINED.
explanation.definitionFit: Dickens's last novel, a mystery left unfinished, has this young man as its title character.

clue.text: Rodent who might qualify for tossing the caber

parts.note: a caber is a tree trunk, a length of timber
to toss something is to throw or fling it

explanation.surface: An animal that might enter the Highland Games.
explanation.walkthrough: The rhyme asks 'How much wood would a woodchuck chuck'; the Highland Games caber toss hurls a tree trunk, so tossing it is chucking wood.
explanation.definitionFit: The North American marmot, or groundhog, is a burrowing rodent.

parts.note: Elaine is the lily maid of the Arthurian town that Malory identified with Guildford in Surrey

explanation.surface: Someone asks where Elaine has gone, guessing the Surrey town.
explanation.walkthrough: Tennyson's Elaine is 'the lily maid' of this Arthurian town, which Malory placed at Guildford, a town in Surrey.
explanation.definitionFit: The Arthurian home of Elaine the lily maid is located by Malory at Guildford.

parts.note: boxing society or company, reread as the enclosures where boxers fight, which share the name of a round band

explanation.surface: The world of professional boxing and its followers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Circles' suggests social sets; boxing arenas carry the name of a round shape even though they are square.
explanation.definitionFit: Boxers fight in roped squares that are still called by the word for circular bands.

parts.note: way reads as manner or habit, but it is the word in a bookmaker's bet covering win or place

explanation.surface: How a betting-shop owner behaves.
explanation.walkthrough: An 'each way' bet at a bookmaker's backs a horse to win or to be placed; 'way' is half the phrase, and the answer the other half.
explanation.definitionFit: Bookmakers take bets covering win and place, called by this word followed by 'way'.

parts.note: seems to ask how few righteous people there were, but refers to the number in Edgar Wallace's thriller title The ... Just Men

explanation.surface: A moral question about how few people are truly righteous.
explanation.walkthrough: Edgar Wallace's 1905 thriller is The Four Just Men; the clue asks the number in the title.
explanation.definitionFit: Edgar Wallace's thriller names a quartet of vigilantes as its just men.

clue.text: Train hedges for the ruined chapel

indicators.note: a ruined building has fallen apart, so the letters of chapel tumble into a new order

explanation.surface: Hedges grown over a tumbledown church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Train' is a verb here: to weave branches into a hedge.
explanation.definitionFit: To interlace branches to form a hedge is to train it.

parts.note: the first word is a detective novel, the second asks literally who did it, meaning who wrote the novel

explanation.surface: A puzzled reader asks who committed the crime in a mystery story.
explanation.walkthrough: The repeated word is read two ways: the detective novel, then 'who done it?', the person who wrote it.
explanation.definitionFit: The writer of a mystery novel is the person who did it, who produced the book.

parts.note: an American word for carry, and also the name of an American carrier bag

explanation.surface: A question about a US airline's business.
explanation.walkthrough: In American usage 'tote' means to carry, and a tote is also a carrier bag.
explanation.definitionFit: In American English one who carries something lugs it, the third person of the verb.

clue.text: "His steeds to water at those springs On flowers that lies "(Cymbeline)

definitions.text: "His steeds to water at those springs On flowers that lies "(Cymbeline)

parts.words: "His steeds to water at those springs On flowers that lies "(Cymbeline)
parts.note: a quotation from the song 'Hark, hark! the lark' in Cymbeline, with the word describing the cup-shaped flowers left out

explanation.surface: A line from Shakespeare's song about the sun watering his horses at dew-filled flowers.
explanation.walkthrough: The gap in Cloten's song 'Hark, hark! the lark' from Cymbeline is filled by the adjective for flowers shaped like cups holding dew.
explanation.definitionFit: Flowers formed like goblets, holding dew like a communion cup, are described with this adjective in Shakespeare's song.

clue.text: You're about right, dear; how miserable !

indicators.note: the endearment goes round the letter for right

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Telling one's darling they are nearly correct, then lamenting the gloom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' puts DEAR around R (right).
explanation.definitionFit: Dreary, gloomy and cheerless: the poetic adjective describes something wretched.

indicators.note: the name reads the same backwards and forwards

parts.note: these definition words give the whole answer, and the answer is itself the palindrome: it reads the same from either end

explanation.surface: A royal whose name reads the same either way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Palindromic' says the name reads the same both ways; several German princes bore it.
explanation.definitionFit: Several German princes, Bismarck among them, bore this given name.

definitions.note: the clue gives the activity; the answer is the person who does it

indicators.note: a variety of something is a different form of it, so the abbreviation's letters are rearranged

parts.note: RETD is the usual abbreviation for retired
an actor is a player on the stage

explanation.surface: A stage veteran who has stepped down now spends his time running others down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Variety' tempts as the music-hall stage beside 'player', but it rearranges RETD (retired) to DETR, followed by ACTOR.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who disparages others behind their backs is a belittler, a practitioner of backbiting.

clue.text: One gifted girl should be fun

parts.note: one means a, the single article
a Muse is one of the nine goddesses of the arts, a woman who inspires gifts

explanation.surface: A talented young woman ought to be good company.
explanation.walkthrough: A Muse is one of the nine daughters of Zeus who inspire the arts, hence a 'gifted girl'.
explanation.definitionFit: To entertain or divert someone is to be fun for them.

definitions.meaning: an outbreak of red spots on the skin

explanation.surface: Someone who acts without thinking breaks out in spots.
explanation.definitionFit: A skin eruption of red spots; and hasty, reckless behaviour, both share the same word.

parts.note: an osteopath manipulates the skeleton, so his machine would jolt the skeleton; the name is that of an early solid-tyred cycle

explanation.surface: What kind of bike a bone doctor rides.
explanation.walkthrough: The Victorian velocipede with iron tyres earned its nickname by jolting riders' skeletons, just what an osteopath does.
explanation.definitionFit: An early iron-tyred velocipede was nicknamed for how it rattled the rider's skeleton.
